Abstract Autoimmune profiling in rats revealed the antioxidant enzyme, peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6), as a target for autoantibodies evoked in response to traumatic brain injury (TBI). Consistent with this proposal, immunohistochemical analysis of rat cerebral cortex demonstrated that PRDX6 is highly expressed in the perivascular space, presumably contained within astrocytic foot processes. Accordingly, an immunosorbent electrochemiluminescence assay was developed for investigating PRDX6 in human samples. PRDX6 was found to be measurable in human blood and highly expressed in human cerebral cortex and platelets. Circulating levels of PRDX6 were elevated fourfold over control values 4 to 24 h following mild-to-moderate TBI. These findings suggest that PRDX6 may serve as a biomarker for TBI and that autoimmune profiling is a viable strategy for the discovery of novel TBI biomarkers. Key words: autoantibodies autoimmune profiling biomarker peroxiredoxin 6 traumatic brain injury Introduction T raumatic injury of the central nervous system elicits a complex cascade of responses that results in activation of microglia and astrocytes, 1–3 inflammation, 4 oxidative stress, 5 opening of the blood–brain barrier, 6 leakage of brain proteins into the systemic circulation, 7 infiltration of leukocytes and immunoglobulins into brain tissue, 8 , 9 and production of cytokines and chemokines. 4 , 8 It has been widely assumed that specific products of any of these processes in the injured brain might find their way into the peripheral circulation, and therefore act as diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers. Accordingly, biomarker research has focused on logical candidates that were selected for study based on informed but a priori judgments. While used extensively, this strategy has not been successful in developing biomarkers for assessing the full range of traumatic brain injury (TBI) severity, particularly mild TBI. 10–13 Here, we have adopted a more global approach in which we used the adaptive immune response to TBI as a pathway for the discovery of novel proteins that may serve as biomarkers for brain injury. We utilized a discovery-based strategy that first involved screening for the expression of autoantibodies in rats in response to controlled cortical injury (CCI). 2 Immunoglobulins from injured rats were used to interrogate the entire rat brain proteome fractionated on large scale two-dimensional (2D) gel electropherograms. Of the approximately 3000 proteins visible in the array, only a small fraction of the proteins exhibited autoreactivity with immunoglobulin G (IgG) from the injured rats than exceeded background observed in controls. We mapped these immunoreactive features to replicate protein gels and identified them by mass spectrometry. 14 One of the most immunoreactive features was identified by mass spectrometry as peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6). PRDX6 is an important anti-oxidant enzyme that hydrolyzes the hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) generated during injury or disease. 15–21 In brain, PRDX6 is primarily expressed in astrocytes, 22 although low levels of expression are also reported in neurons. 23 PRDX6 also is found in the periphery, including in the lung, kidney, skin, and neutrophils. The protein also is found in several forms of cancer. 24–26 While several proteomics studies have identified PRDX6 as a central nervous system protein and have shown its release into cerebral spinal fluid following spinal cord injury, 27–30 these studies did not explore the possibility of its role as a blood-borne candidate biomarker for TBI. The present investigation demonstrates for the first time that PRDX6 is a normal constituent of human plasma where its levels are acutely elevated following mild-to-moderate TBI. While the specificity of this response to TBI has yet to be determined, these findings indicate that PRDX6 may contribute to a biomarker signature for acute mild brain injury.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigates the discovery of novel traumatic brain injury (TBI) biomarkers using autoimmune profiling in both rat models and human patients. It details methodologies for sample preparation, protein analysis via 2D gel electrophoresis, immunoprofiling, and the development of an immunosorbent electrochemiluminescence assay (IEA) for peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6). The main findings establish PRDX6 as a candidate TBI biomarker, showing its astrocytic expression, TBI-induced autoantibody reactivity in rats, gender differences in baseline human plasma levels, and a significant, persistent approximately fourfold elevation of circulating PRDX6 in humans following mild-to-moderate TBI, which is proportional to injury severity and independent of imaging findings. The study also acknowledges S100B and GFAP as other relevant TBI indicators.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) and Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) injury model
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Human TBI was observed as mild-to-moderate (median GCS 15), with plasma collected at 4-24 hours and 2-7 days post-injury; no direct manipulation or controlled dose was applied, though PRDX6 response correlated with injury severity. In rat models, severe CCI injury was induced using a stereotaxic impactor with a 5 mm impactor at a 20-degree angle to a depth of 2 mm at 5 m/sec with a dwell time of 500 msec to maximize autoimmune response. No specific dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported for either human TBI or rat CCI, beyond PRDX6 response proportionality in humans.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Human plasma, human serum, human cerebral cortex, human platelets, rat cerebral cortex, rat serum/plasma
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level, Protein Expression (Immunohistochemistry), Protein Concentration (IEA), Autoantibody reactivity

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PRDX6 is highly expressed in rat brain astrocytes (perivascular space) and human cerebral cortex (approx. 940 ng/mg soluble protein), and human platelets (approx. 500 ng/mg soluble protein). Autoantibodies against PRDX6 are enhanced in rat serum following CCI. In humans, basal plasma levels are significantly higher in females (141-178 ng/mL) than males (43-65 ng/mL, p<0.001). Coagulation significantly reduces measured PRDX6 levels in serum compared to plasma, especially in females. Following mild-to-moderate TBI, circulating human plasma PRDX6 is elevated approximately fourfold over control values (from 93±18 ng/mL to 322±15 ng/mL at admission), persisting up to seven days (372±15 ng/mL, p>0.01). While absolute elevated levels post-TBI did not differ by gender (males: 351±17 ng/mL vs. females: 312±25 ng/mL), fold increases were approximately sevenfold in males and twofold in females. No difference was observed between image-positive and image-negative TBI patients. The assay has a lower limit of detection of 0.7 ng/mL and quantitation of 1 ng/mL.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A crucial antioxidant enzyme involved in hydrolyzing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) during injury and disease. It is highly expressed in astrocytes, particularly in the perivascular space, and acts as an autoantigen target following TBI, with oxidative stress potentially influencing its antigenicity. It also functions as a circulating protein whose levels are influenced by gender and sample preparation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Mild-to-moderate Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) in humans (acute phase at 4-24 hours post-injury, persisting up to seven days), Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) in rats, and basal physiological conditions including gender differences and sample preparation effects (plasma vs. serum).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A promising candidate biomarker for the diagnosis and assessment of Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), particularly mild TBI. Its acute plasma response is proportional to injury severity, making it useful as an injury severity marker. It indicates a TBI-induced autoimmune response, highlights the importance of gender and sample type (plasma vs. serum) for accurate measurement, and can indicate injury presence and persistence for at least seven days, though it doesn't distinguish TBI with visible imaging abnormalities.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Responses in serum titers of anti-S100B antibodies were proportional to the number and severity of hits experienced. S100B protein levels increase in blood in response to TBI.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A long-recognized TBI biomarker, highly expressed in astrocytes. Released upon repetitive disruption of the blood-brain barrier, leading to immune activation and autoantibody formation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Repeated sub-concussive hits to the head (e.g., in collegiate football players); Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Candidate TBI biomarker; autoantibodies against S100B correlate with changes in brain structure detected by diffusion tensor imaging, indicating its role in TBI assessment.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: TBI induces the expression of autoantibodies against GFAP and its breakdown products. GFAP protein levels increase in blood in response to TBI.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Highly expressed in astrocytes and a constituent of blood. Autoantibodies against GFAP are induced by TBI.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Candidate TBI biomarker; autoantibodies against GFAP are indicative of TBI.
